extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and creative writers studying poetics, drama, and characterisation
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for creating and evaluating comic and tragic characterization, plot-cohesion, and poetic truth derived from Aristotle and classical Greek practice. Useful for dramatists and fiction writers aiming to balance universality and individuality in character and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation by suppression of accidental features
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject-matter already possesses grandeur or dignity, its dominant characteristics become more salient by the suppression of accidental features, producing an ideal form with added beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: portrait-painting and tragic leading characters; eliminate the accidental to discover higher beauty and perfection. Use suppression to universalise and embellish the subject rather than to invent flawless beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero: elevated but flawed
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero is not free from faults or failings; a character may have defects yet possess moral nobility that entitles him to rank as ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heighten some commanding faculties provided the equipoise of character is not disturbed (Achilles as an example). Avoid making the hero flawless—retain balance so the character remains typically human.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal is universal, not merely perfect virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal is what is raised above the trivial and accidental by virtue of a universal element which answers to the true idea of the object; aesthetic 'ought' is not moral perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idealisation should aim at the noblest and fairest form consistent with artistic laws, not moral absolutism. Preserve a universal element that transcends individual limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's scope: focus on follies and foibles
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy concerns itself with the follies, foibles, flaws and imperfections of mankind and thus cannot idealise or universalise its object in the same manner as tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibit imperfections as aspects of common humanity to be laughed at rather than hated. Comedy is limited to presenting those negative, often transient aspects of life that provoke mirth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective inclusion of imperfections
rubrics_metrics.description: Art must decide which imperfections are accidental, abnormal, or unworthy of lasting embodiment, and which are permanent features of humanity suited to representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This determination varies across historical stages and across artistic forms. Include only those defects that serve the work's artistic purpose and type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ludicrous defined: painless defect, not malice
rubrics_metrics.description: The ludicrous 'consists in some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive' and does not imply malice; it provokes laughter without inflicting harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use defects, deformities, incongruities, or disproportionate elements that are 'not painful or destructive' (comic mask example). Avoid personal malice or cruelty as the core of comic effect—malice may season but is not essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity and transition as source of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity produces the ludicrous only when there is a transition or change of mood resulting in the discovery of an unexpected resemblance or unlikeness; the pleasure arises from the shock of surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft moments where expectation is shifted to reveal an incongruity; blend contrasted feelings (sympathy, malice, detachment) but ensure the transition produces painless surprise rather than harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of personal satire in 'pure' comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine comedy, as idealised by Aristotle, banishes personal satire and galling caricature, favouring generalised types over invective directed at individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer types and humorous situations that represent the universal human condition rather than lampooning named persons; use subtle innuendo rather than coarse abusive language for refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expressive or type-names to signal universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often uses names which are etymologically or conventionally significant (e.g., 'the Boor', 'the Parasite') so that a single name evokes the character-type rather than a historical individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign names that signal occupation, condition, or dominant humour; ideally, names should emerge after plotting so they mark the type rather than tie the plot to historical specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification and allegory to embody ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Some comic practice personifies abstractions (Justice, Riches, Logic) and dramatizes opposing principles as an agôn (debate), making characters embodiments of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bold personification deliberately when you want to foreground ideological conflict or satirical argument, but be aware this may sacrifice individual consistency for allegorical clarity (Aristophanes model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot unity and moral probability
rubrics_metrics.description: In Middle and New Comedy the action acquires beginning, middle, and end; character and action become more intimately united and moral probability replaces arbitrary sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for coherent plot structure where motives and consequences cohere; avoid loose episodic sequences unless deliberately invoking the older lampooning style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pure realism and pure symbolism; seek poetic truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure literal realism (mere sensory jugglery) and pure fantastical symbolism (impossible hybrids) are forbidden; poetic truth allows irrational or impossible elements only when they cohere and render the fiction plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present impossible or magical elements with internal coherence so that the whole appears plausible (Odyssey example). Do not rely on spectacle or grotesque hybrids that violate the work's internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure, restraint, and harmonious expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek imaginative ideal values temperate strength, self-restraint, and harmonious expression—expression without effort or ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer harmony and measured presentation over dazzling effects; give the audience truthful, balanced perception rather than overwhelming sensory display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy tends to abstract a single dominant trait
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic character-drawing often embodies a dominant characteristic or leading passion so overwhelmingly that 'the single attribute becomes the man', which risks caricature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If isolating a trait for comic effect, be conscious of the risk of impossible simplicity; use supporting details to keep the caricature artistically productive rather than merely flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour enriched by sympathy broadens universality
rubrics_metrics.description: When humour is combined with sympathy (the deeper kind of humour), it rediscovers incongruities without triumphal malice and can generalise human contradictions more profoundly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend humour and sympathy to create characters who are both comic and deeply human (examples: Don Quixote, Uncle Toby). This approach enables comedy to approach tragic insight and produce pathos alongside mirth.
